passage: Monday: Himani held out a spoonful of soup and Pallavi, two, shook her head firmly from side to side, lips shut. Himani put the spoon down. Wednesday: a visitor offered a plastic toy and Pallavi shook her head and hid behind the sofa, so Himani thanked the visitor and said Pallavi would look later. Friday: Himani held up two pairs of shoes. Pallavi shook her head at the blue ones and pointed at the red. “Red it is,” said Himani.

qa.q: Which pair of shoes did Pallavi choose on Friday?
qa.a: The red ones, which she pointed at after shaking her head at the blue.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's head shaking seem to say on the three days?
qa.a: On the soup and toy days it seems to say she does not want it now, and on Friday it shows she prefers red. She may also just have liked the feeling of deciding.

qa.q: What made Himani's responses helpful?
qa.a: She respected the refusal without a fight and gave a choice on Friday, which let Pallavi say what she wanted.

qa.q: How might the visitor feel when Pallavi shakes her head?
qa.a: The visitor may feel a little awkward, but Himani's thanks shows it is not personal.

grounding: A toddler shakes her head to refuse before she can speak clearly, and an adult responds with respect.

passage: Wasim peeled a banana in the flat's small kitchen and held it towards Devika's high chair. She shook her head, once each way, then again, lips pressed tight, eyes on his face. “No banana?” he said. She shook her head again. “Okay. Apple?” Devika looked at the apple bowl and nodded so hard her curls bounced. Wasim laughed, cut a slice and gave it to her. She ate it, happily swinging her legs.

qa.q: What did Devika refuse in the kitchen?
qa.a: The banana that Wasim peeled.

qa.q: What does the head shaking show Devika wants?
qa.a: It shows she does not want the banana and wants a say in what she eats. It might also mean she is full or just wanted something different.

qa.q: What could Wasim try if she refuses the apple too?
qa.a: He could stay calm, put the food away and offer again later without pressure.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when she says no with her head?
qa.a: He may be a little amused and proud that she can already let him know her mind. 😊

grounding: A toddler shakes her head to say no and show her wish for control, and an adult responds with respect.

passage: Nursery note, Thursday. Abhinav, two, turned his whole head toward me each time I began the counting song, eyes bright, and edged closer on the mat. At lunch he took three spoonfuls of dal and rice, then turned his head away and held his lips together. I lowered the spoon and said, “All done?” He looked back at me and smiled. I put the bowl aside. He ate a banana later. 🙂 Yusuf

qa.q: How many spoonfuls did Abhinav take at lunch before turning away?
qa.a: Three spoonfuls of dal and rice.

qa.q: What might Abhinav's head turn away from the spoon mean, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It most likely means he had eaten enough and wanted to stop. It could also mean he wanted something different, but his smile afterwards showed no distress.

qa.q: Why was Yusuf's response helpful?
qa.a: Yusuf respected the turn-away, which shows Abhinav that his signals count, and still offered food later.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when the spoon goes down?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and understood, and be more willing to eat again at the next meal.

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and turns away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the signal.

passage: On the mud verandah, Kiran hummed an old lullaby while she plaited her own hair. Her granddaughter Salma, two, who had been playing with pebbles, turned her head toward the sound and crawled over into her lap. Kiran held a cup of warm milk to her lips. Salma took two sips and then turned her face to the wall, lips closed. Kiran waited, then set the cup on the step. “Later, then,” she said, and went on humming.

qa.q: What did Salma turn her head toward on the verandah?
qa.a: The sound of Kiran humming an old lullaby.

qa.q: What could Salma's turn to the wall mean, and what else might it be?
qa.a: It probably means she was done with the milk. It could also mean she was too warm or wanted to keep listening to the song.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that helped?
qa.a: She waited, did not push the cup and kept humming, so Salma stayed close and comfortable.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when her signal is respected?
qa.a: She may feel that turning away is enough to be heard, which builds trust that she does not have to cry to be understood. 🙂

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the turn-away.

passage: A dog barked hard behind the mud wall, and Vikas, two, froze in the yard. His shoulders shot up towards his ears and his fists tightened, eyes on the wall. Sunaina scooped him up. “It's only Motu next door.” She walked around the yard, patting his back. Slowly his shoulders dropped, his hands opened and his head rested in the crook of her neck. When the dog barked again, Vikas only sighed and stayed loose in her arms.

qa.q: Where did Vikas's shoulders go when the dog barked?
qa.a: They shot up towards his ears.

qa.q: What does the change in Vikas's shoulders show he feels?
qa.a: The tight shoulders show fear, and the loose ones in Sunaina's arms show he feels safe. Tense shoulders might also mean pain, but the barking makes fear more likely.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do to help him with barking dogs?
qa.a: She could stay close when they bark, keep a calm voice and let him look at the dog from a safe distance.

qa.q: What might Sunaina feel while carrying him?
qa.a: She may feel protective and glad he trusts her arms to calm him.

grounding: A toddler's tense shoulders in fear relax in a caregiver's arms, showing safety.

passage: The market in Lagos was crowded and loud. Yosef, two, rode on his mother Ada's hip, his shoulders stiff and high, hands gripping her blouse, eyes darting from stall to stall. Ada moved out to the edge of the square and bounced him gently. She hummed and pointed to a stall of oranges. After a minute his shoulders sank, one hand relaxed and he leaned his weight into her. By the time they reached the bus, he was almost asleep.

qa.q: Where was Yosef riding in the market?
qa.a: On his mother Ada's hip.

qa.q: What do Yosef's high stiff shoulders suggest, and what changed?
qa.a: They suggest he was uneasy in the crowd, and the dropped shoulders later show he felt safe. Stiff shoulders can also be a sign of pain, so Ada watched the whole picture.

qa.q: What could Ada do before the next busy market visit?
qa.a: She could plan a shorter trip, carry him close and stop at quiet spots to let him settle.

qa.q: What might the market feel like to Yosef?
qa.a: It may seem loud, bright and full of strangers, so being held close is the safe place he needs. 🤍

grounding: A toddler's tense shoulders in a crowd become relaxed and dropped in his mother's arms, showing safety.

passage: Tuesday: A neighbour came to visit and Gopika, two, hunched her shoulders up to her ears and pressed against her mother Sangeeta's legs. Sangeeta let her hide. Wednesday: the neighbour returned. Gopika peeked from behind Sangeeta, shoulders still raised, then ducked away. Thursday: the neighbour sat quietly with tea, not looking at her. Gopika's shoulders lowered a little and she walked over holding out her doll. The neighbour said “Hello, doll,” and Gopika almost smiled.

qa.q: What did Gopika hold out to the neighbour on Thursday?
qa.a: Her doll.

qa.q: What do the raised shoulders on Tuesday suggest Gopika feels?
qa.a: They suggest shyness or unease with a stranger. It might also mean she was tired, but her steady change over three days points to warming up.

qa.q: What helped Gopika warm up?
qa.a: Sangeeta let her hide, and the neighbour sat quietly instead of crowding her, so she could approach when ready.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel after the first visit?
qa.a: The neighbour may feel a little rejected, but understanding that Gopika is only shy helps them stay patient.

grounding: A toddler hunches her shoulders when shy with a stranger, and letting her warm up over days is respectful.

passage: In the corner shop of their colony, Karthik, two, stood beside his mother Sabina, his shoulders up around his ears. The shopkeeper leaned over the counter, smiling, and said, “Hello, little man!” Karthik turned his face into Sabina's leg. “He's shy today,” she said. The shopkeeper straightened and went on counting change without any fuss. Karthik peeked from the folds of her kurta, still hunched. On the way out he gave a tiny wave over his shoulder.

qa.q: Where were Karthik and Sabina?
qa.a: At the corner shop in their colony.

qa.q: What does the wave on the way out suggest about how Karthik felt?
qa.a: It suggests he warmed up a little, even though he stayed hunched and hidden at first. It might also just be a habit of waving bye-bye.

qa.q: What could Sabina do to help him with strangers?
qa.a: She could let him watch from her side, greet people herself and never push him to speak.

qa.q: What might the shopkeeper think about Karthik?
qa.a: The shopkeeper may be amused or a little disappointed, but Sabina's words show it is just shyness, and they carry on without fuss. 🙂

grounding: A toddler raises and hunches the shoulders when shy with a stranger, and letting him warm up is respectful.

subtype: Raising arms to be picked up [Expressing]
passage: At the gate of the market, Rajni was juggling two bags and her phone. Vishal, two, tugged at her kurta, then stretched both arms straight up and looked into her eyes. “Up.” She checked the bags and crouched. “Okay, come.” She lifted him onto her hip and he put his head on her shoulder, warm and quiet. His legs dangled and he sighed once. Rajni kept the bags on her other arm and walked on.

qa.q: What was Rajni carrying when Vishal raised his arms?
qa.a: Two bags and her phone.

qa.q: What might Vishal's raised arms and look mean he wanted?
qa.a: They show he wanted to be lifted and close to her. It could also be tiredness from walking, or wanting a better view.

qa.q: What could Rajni do if her hands were too full?
qa.a: She could kneel, hug him for a moment and tell him she will lift him as soon as she puts the bags down.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when she lifts him?
qa.a: He may feel safe and looked after because his request was answered.

grounding: A toddler raises both arms to be picked up, a clear request for closeness that the adult answers.

subtype: Raising arms to be picked up [Expressing]
passage:
“Chaitanya, we're at the top of the stairs,” said Lalit. “Good walking.”
Chaitanya looked up at him and lifted both arms.
“Up?”
“You want me to carry you?”
“Up, Papa.”
“All right, all right.” He lifted her and she wound her arms round his neck.
“Tired?” he asked.
She nodded against his shoulder.
“Then we'll rest a bit,” said Lalit, and sat down on the step with her.

qa.q: Where were Lalit and Chaitanya when she raised her arms?
qa.a: At the top of the stairs.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's raised arms and nod show she wanted?
qa.a: They show she wanted to be carried and was tired. She might also simply have wanted closeness with Papa.

qa.q: What could Lalit do on other tiring days?
qa.a: He could plan rest breaks or let her walk part of the way and carry her the rest.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya feel when he sits down with her?
qa.a: She may feel cared for because Papa noticed her tiredness and stopped for her.

grounding: A toddler raises both arms to be lifted and shows tiredness and a wish for closeness.

passage: In a park in Berlin, Rosa, two, spotted her mother Clara at the far gate. Her arms flew wide and started flapping, her whole body wiggled and she ran across the grass shouting “Mama, Mama!” At the last moment she crashed into Clara's legs, arms still open. Clara laughed and swept her up. “You're so excited to see me!” she said. Rosa squealed and flapped her arms again, one hand catching Clara's hair.

qa.q: Where did Rosa see her mother?
qa.a: At the far gate of a park in Berlin.

qa.q: What do Rosa's flapping arms show she was feeling?
qa.a: They show joy and excitement about seeing Clara. Flapping arms could also be a burst of energy after a long wait.

qa.q: How could Clara help Rosa learn about the feeling?
qa.a: She named it, as she did by saying “You're so excited”, which gives Rosa a word to link to the feeling. 🙂

qa.q: What might a stranger nearby think seeing the flying arms?
qa.a: They might wonder if she is going to hit someone, but the laughter and joyful shouting make it clear it is a greeting.

grounding: A toddler spreads and flaps her arms with excitement at a favourite person, showing joy and energy rather than aggression.

passage: Our garden bench faces the lawn, so I saw everything. Pooja, about two, spotted her grandmother Vasudha coming through the gate with a shopping bag. Both of her arms shot out sideways and she flapped them, running in a big loop before coming at her at full speed. For a moment it looked wild, but her face was all grin and Vasudha simply opened her arms. I can't know what Pooja thought, but the flapping was plain gladness.

qa.q: Where did the narrator watch Pooja?
qa.a: From a garden bench facing the lawn.

qa.q: Why did the narrator decide the flapping was gladness and not aggression?
qa.a: Pooja was grinning and running to Vasudha, who opened her arms without alarm. The narrator admits they cannot know what Pooja was thinking.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do to help if Pooja runs too fast?
qa.a: She could crouch and hold her arms out so Pooja slows into the hug, and show gently how to stop.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel to be greeted this way?
qa.a: She may feel loved and pleased, and even if tired after shopping, the greeting lifts her mood.

grounding: A toddler flaps her arms with excitement toward a favourite person, seen by an observer who reads it as joy, not aggression.

passage:
“Santosh, the last block!” Lalit said. Santosh set it on top of the tower and it stayed.
He looked at the tower, then at his father, then began to clap, fast, with a big open mouth.
“You did it! That's clapping for you!”
“Again,” Santosh said, and clapped again.
“Shall we clap together?”
Lalit clapped too, and they clapped in the same rhythm, badly, laughing.
Santosh flopped back on the mat, still clapping.

qa.q: What did Santosh place on top of the tower?
qa.a: The last block.

qa.q: What do Santosh's claps show he feels, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: They show pride and joy at the finished tower. He might also be copying the clapping his father does at his successes.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next?
qa.a: He could build another tower with Santosh and clap for tries as well as for finished towers.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel while clapping with him?
qa.a: He may feel happy and close to his son, because they share the moment.

grounding: A toddler claps at his own achievement and shares the joy with a parent who claps too.

passage: Toddler room note, Monday. Baljeet, almost two, clapped his hands the moment we began the morning song, first watching me, then laughing when the other children joined. Later, when Meher finished her puzzle, Baljeet clapped for her, even though he had not done it himself. He looked at me to see whether I was clapping too. I was. We ended up with a room full of clapping toddlers. 🙂 Lokesh

qa.q: What did Baljeet clap for after the morning song?
qa.a: He clapped for Meher when she finished her puzzle.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling as he claps, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He seems happy and part of the group, shown by his laughing and his look to Lokesh to check that Lokesh was clapping too. He might partly be copying the others.

qa.q: How could Lokesh keep this happy routine going?
qa.a: Lokesh could make clapping a regular part of songs and successes so that children share joy together.

qa.q: What might Meher feel when Baljeet claps for her?
qa.a: She may feel proud and noticed, because a friend shared her success.

grounding: A toddler claps at a song and a friend's achievement, sharing joy and copying others in a happy social routine.

passage: Nursery note, Wednesday. Deepika, nearly two, reached both hands towards my beaker and made a grunting sound, eyes on it. When I put it in reach, her hands closed round it. Later, as her mother's shadow crossed the door, Deepika reached with both hands again and clasped her mother's fingers tightly, holding on all the way to the coat hooks. I said, “You wanted the cup, and you wanted Mummy.” 🙂 Trisha

qa.q: What did Deepika reach for first?
qa.a: Her carer's beaker.

qa.q: What do Deepika's reaching hands show in each case?
qa.a: At the beaker they show a wish for the cup, and with her mother they show closeness and love. She might also have been reaching just from habit.

qa.q: What is Trisha doing that helps Deepika's development?
qa.a: Trisha names what Deepika wants in words, which links her gestures with language.

qa.q: How might Deepika's mother feel when her fingers are clasped?
qa.a: She may feel very loved and reassured that her daughter wants to be near her.

grounding: A toddler reaches for an object and clasps a parent's hand, showing desire and affection, and the adult names the meaning.

passage: At the temple fair, the crowd surged and Baljeet took Kiran's small hand in his. Kiran, two, curled her fingers tightly round his thumb and would not let go. Then she saw the toffee stall and stretched her other arm out, fingers opening and closing. “Toffee, toffee.” Baljeet bought her one. She held it with the other hand while her thumb-hand stayed clasped on him, all the way past the bullock-cart rides.

qa.q: What did Kiran reach toward at the fair?
qa.a: The toffee stall.

qa.q: What does Kiran's tight hold on Baljeet's thumb show?
qa.a: It shows she felt safe holding him in the crowd and wanted him near. It could also be that she was afraid of being pushed by the crowd.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do to keep her feeling secure?
qa.a: He can hold her hand or carry her through the crowd and tell her where they are going.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel when she reaches for the toffee and still holds on?
qa.a: He may feel amused and warm, seeing that she wants both her treat and him.

grounding: A toddler reaches for a wanted object and clasps an adult's hand, showing desire and affection.

subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage: On the bus in Toronto, Tariq, two, sat on his caregiver Rosa's lap and curled his finger towards a pigeon on the window ledge, “Come, come.” The pigeon stayed put. Then the driver called “Ready?” and Tariq put up a thumb, copying Rosa. The driver gave a thumb back and grinned. Tariq looked at his own thumb, delighted, and did it again to a woman across the aisle. She lifted a thumb too. Rosa laughed. He did not know what it meant, only what it made happen.

qa.q: Who did Tariq beckon at the bus window?
qa.a: A pigeon on the window ledge.

qa.q: What does Tariq's delighted look at his thumb suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he enjoys the response he gets more than knowing the meaning of the gesture. He might also just like copying Rosa.

qa.q: What could Rosa do to help Tariq understand these gestures?
qa.a: Rosa could say “good” or “come here” as she gestures so that words and movements go together.

qa.q: How might the woman across the aisle feel about the thumb?
qa.a: She may feel touched or amused by a child's friendly gesture and enjoy returning it.

grounding: A toddler copies beckoning and thumbs-up gestures from adults without full understanding, and the meaning follows the response he sees.

subtype: Beckoning and thumbs-up copied from adults [Expressing]
passage: From the vegetable stall I watched Tenzin, two, on his grandmother Nirmala's hip. He curled his finger in the air towards a passing cow, “Come,” though the cow ignored him. When Nirmala bought him a biscuit, he raised his thumb high because she did, and grinned. The vendor gave him a thumb back. I don't think Tenzin knows what it means yet, but the reaction made him do it again. Nirmala looked at me, laughing. “He copies everything.”

qa.q: What did Tenzin do towards the passing cow?
qa.a: He curled his finger in the air and said “Come”.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Tenzin understands about the thumb?
qa.a: The narrator thinks he does not know the meaning yet, but repeats it because people react warmly. That is only the narrator's impression.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do to build on the gesture?
qa.a: She could say “good, thank you” with the thumb so the gesture and words go together.

qa.q: How might the vendor feel when Tenzin gives him a thumbs-up?
qa.a: The vendor may feel amused and pleased that a small child treats him as a friend.

grounding: A toddler copies come-here and thumbs-up gestures from adults, and the narrator sees that the meaning follows the reaction.

passage: Toddler room note, Friday. When Nikita's father collected her, Nikita waved bye-bye at me with her whole arm and said “Ba!” Earlier in the garden she had stopped, pointed a finger at an aeroplane and looked back at me, eyebrows up. I said, “Aeroplane! Up in the sky.” She pointed again and repeated “Aa-pane.” I will keep naming what she points at, and tell her father about this new word. 🙂 Gautam

qa.q: What did Nikita point at in the garden?
qa.a: An aeroplane in the sky.

qa.q: What did Nikita want when she pointed and looked back at Gautam?
qa.a: She probably wanted to share her interest and hear the name of the aeroplane. She might also just have been checking Gautam's face.

qa.q: What is Gautam's plan and why does it help?
qa.a: Gautam will keep naming what she points at, which teaches new words and shows that her gestures are heard.

qa.q: How might Nikita's father feel hearing about the new word?
qa.a: He may be proud and pleased, and try naming things with her at home too.

grounding: A toddler waves bye-bye and points to share interest, and the teacher responds by naming the object.

passage: Tejas, two, sat on his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders on the road to the bus stand. A buffalo stood by the roadside and Tejas pointed with a fat finger, looking down at Hrithik. “Bhains,” said Hrithik. “Big buffalo.” Tejas pointed again and said “Ba.” When the bus arrived and Hrithik's brother climbed on, Tejas waved his whole hand until the bus turned the corner.

qa.q: What did Tejas point at by the roadside?
qa.a: A buffalo.

qa.q: What might Tejas have wanted when he pointed and looked down?
qa.a: He probably wanted to share what he saw and get a name for it. He could also have been checking that Hrithik had noticed.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do next to help Tejas learn more?
qa.a: He could keep naming things Tejas points at and wait for him to try the words himself.

qa.q: What might the brother on the bus feel when Tejas waves?
qa.a: He may feel warmed by the wave and wave back, since the child is saying goodbye in his way.

grounding: A toddler waves bye-bye and points to share interest, and the adult responds by naming the object.
